controlScores.description: Research has found that when periodic password resets are enforced, passwords become less secure. Users tend to pick a weaker password and vary it slightly for each reset. If a user creates a strong password (long, complex and without any pragmatic words present) it should remain just as strong in the future as it is today. It is Microsoft's official security position to not expire passwords periodically without a specific reason, and recommends that cloud-only tenants set the password policy to never expire.

controlScores.description:
Having more than one global administrator helps if you are unable to fulfill the needs or obligations of your organization. It's important to have a delegate or an emergency account someone from your team can access if necessary. It also allows admins the ability to monitor each other for signs of a breach.

Note:

According to CIS O365 Benchmark 2.0.0, the suggestion is to have between two to four global admins. Currently, the condition to comply is to have more than one global administrator - This security recommendation will be updated accordingly to CIS benchmark in the future.

Rationale:

If there is only one global tenant administrator, he or she can perform malicious activity without the possibility of being discovered by another Test User 1. If there are numerous global tenant administrators, the more likely it is that one of their accounts will be successfully breached by an external attacker.

Ensure that your administrators can accomplish their work with the least amount of privilege assigned to their account. Assigning users roles like Password Administrator or Exchange Online Administrator, instead of Global Administrator, reduces the likelihood of a global administrative privileged account being breached.

controlScores.description: By restricting anonymous users from joining Microsoft Teams meetings, you have full control over meeting access. Anonymous users may not be from your organization and could have joined for malicious purposes, such as gaining information about your organization through conversations.
Dial-in users aren’t authenticated though the Teams app. Increase the security of your meetings by preventing these unknown users from bypassing the lobby and immediately joining the meeting.

External participants are users that are outside your organization. Limiting their permission to share content, add new users, and more protects your organization’s information from data leaks, inappropriate content being shared, or malicious actors joining the meeting.

If anonymous users are allowed to start meetings, they can admit any users from the lobbies, authenticated or otherwise. Anonymous users haven’t been authenticated, which can increase the risk of data leakage.

Users who aren’t invited to a meeting shouldn’t be let in automatically, because it increases the risk of data leaks, inappropriate content being shared, or malicious actors joining. If only invited users are automatically admitted, then users who weren’t invited will be sent to a meeting lobby. The host can then decide whether or not to let them in.
Only allow users with presenter rights to share content during meetings. Restricting who can present limits meeting disruptions and reduces the risk of unwanted or inappropriate content being shared.

The Remote Registry service allows remote users to read and modify registry settings over the network. You can disable this service to reduce the remote attack surface, and to prevent unauthorized configuration changes, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

When Remote Registry is enabled, attackers can remotely connect to the registry of a device and alter security controls, establish persistence, or weaken defenses.

Productivity considerations:
When you disable Remote Registry, this may affect environments that remotely read or write configuration through the Windows registry. Tools used to administer DFS Namespaces from another machine may fail to operate, for example, DFS Management MMC (Dfsmgmt.msc), Dfsutil.exe, Dfscmd.exe, and Dfsdiag.exe.

In many domain-controller deployments, the DFS Namespace (Dfs) relies on reading or updating registry-based configuration remotely. When Dfs is disabled, the dependency chain can break, leading to namespace resolution failures (for example: \\domain\<dfsroot>) and potential impact to SYSVOL and GPO processing.

To avoid this type of impact to productivity, you can perform DFS management locally on the server or temporarily enable the Remote Registry service. Learn more about how to assess productivity impact, monitor event logs, and remediate issues.

Remote registry access can be abused by attackers to make unauthorized configuration changes, establish persistence, or move laterally within the network.

Examples of attacks include:
  • Credential theft by reading stored credentials or password hashes from registry locations, which can later be used for impersonation or lateral movement.
  • Disabling security tools by modifying registry keys related to Windows Defender or other antivirus configurations.
  • Remote code execution by altering registry entries tied to scheduled tasks or startup programs, enabling malicious payloads to run automatically.
  • Lateral movement through registry-based persistence mechanisms or remote configuration changes.

This configuration enforces that LDAP servers (e.g., domain controllers) require signed requests from clients. Signing validates the integrity and origin of LDAP traffic, preventing tampering or spoofing of authentication requests.

Note on productivity impact:
Some environments may still rely on LDAP for certain processes. More details on how to check productivity impact and monitor event logs can be found here.


If unsigned LDAP communication is allowed, attackers can exploit it to alter traffic, forge requests, or impersonate users, leading to privilege escalation and unauthorized access.

Channel binding ties the LDAP authentication layer to the underlying secure TLS channel, protecting against attacks that spoof or hijack sessions.
It ensures that both ends of the connection verify the security context and that the client is communicating with the intended server.
This setting helps enforce session integrity, particularly for LDAPS connections, by mitigating credential replay and man-in-the-middle risks. Note on productivity impact:
Some environments may still rely on LDAP for certain processes. More details on how to check productivity impact and monitor event logs can be found here.


Without channel binding, attackers can spoof sessions or downgrade security, leading to credential theft or impersonation. Channel binding enforces stricter validation of encrypted sessions.

Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) enables remote access to devices, including the ability to transfer files between remote and local machines. Blocking the ability to transfer files over RDP reduces the risk of data exfiltration and prevents attackers from moving malicious files into the environment.
Without this setting, attackers can use RDP sessions to bypass security controls and transfer sensitive data or malware.
Allowing transferring files over RDP exposes devices to potential data theft and malware propagation. Attackers can leverage RDP sessions to exfiltrate confidential information or introduce malicious files, increasing the risk of lateral movement and compromise.

Prevents the Microsoft HTML Application Host (mshta.exe) from establishing outbound network connections using Windows Firewall. The control maintains the legitimate local functionality of mshta.exe while blocking its ability to download remote content or communicate with external servers, significantly reducing the attack surface commonly exploited by threat actors.
Microsoft HTML Application Host (mshta.exe) presents a significant security risk. Threat actors exploit mshta.exe as it's a native, signed Microsoft binary (LOLBin), bypasses application allow-listing, executes scripts from remote URLs, operates within user security context, and has minimal logging. Blocking outbound connections from mshta.exe disrupts attack chains, prevents C2 communications, blocks data exfiltration and forces attackers to use other techniques.

Identifies internet-facing devices in your environment and reduces exposure where possible.

Defender defines Internet-facing devices as devices that are accessible from outside the organizational network. These devices can either receive inbound connections over TCP or are identified as reachable over UDP. This determination is based on a combination of external scanning, which identifies devices that can be reached from the public Internet, and device network signals that Defender collects. Defender uses these signals to detect incoming external traffic that reaches internal devices.

  • To reduce unnecessary exposure to your assets, review the flagged assets to confirm that only devices that need to be exposed are reachable. Based on this review, take action to remove unnecessary exposure.

Note: This recommendation applies to supported Windows client and Windows Server devices. Supported versions include Windows 10, version 1607 and earlier; Windows 10, version 1809 and later; and Windows 11.


Attackers and automated scanners can continuously discover, scan, and probe Internet-facing devices. These devices become prime targets for credential brute-forcing, exploitation of unpatched vulnerabilities, and initial access for ransomware and hands-on-keyboard intrusions. A single exposed device with a weak password, outdated software, or a known CVE can serve as an entry point into the internal network, leading to lateral movement, privilege escalation, data exfiltration, and full domain compromise.

If you're a Microsoft 365 customer with mailboxes in Exchange Online or a standalone Exchange Online Protection (EOP) customer without Exchange Online mailboxes, EOP offers multiple ways of ensuring that users will receive email from trusted senders. These options include Exchange mail flow rules (also known as transport rules), Outlook Safe Senders, the IP Allow List (connection filtering), and allowed sender lists or allowed domain lists in anti-spam policies. Collectively, you can think of these options as safe sender lists.

The available safe sender lists are described in the following list in order from most recommended to least recommended:
1. Mail flow rules
2. Outlook Safe Senders
3. IP Allow List (connection filtering)
4. Allowed sender lists or allowed domain lists (anti-spam policies)

Since the IP Allow List doesn't prevent malware or high confidence phishing messages from being filtered, this creates a high risk of attackers successfully delivering email to an inbox that would otherwise be filtered.

Additionally, when mailbox audit logging is turned on, some actions performed by administrators, delegates, and owners are logged by default.

Rationale:

Starting in January 2019, Microsoft is turning on mailbox audit logging by default for all organizations.

This means that certain actions performed by mailbox owners, delegates, and admins are automatically logged, and the corresponding mailbox audit records will be available when you search for them in the mailbox audit log. The remaining mailbox types require auditing to be turned on at the mailbox level: Resource Mailboxes, Public Folder Mailboxes, and DiscoverySearch Mailbox.

Whether it is for regulatory compliance or for tracking unauthorized configuration changes in Microsoft 365, enabling mailbox auditing allows for Microsoft 365 back office teams to run security operations, forensics or general investigations on mailbox activities.

controlScores.description:
Enable Windows LAPS or legacy Microsoft LAPS so that local administrator passwords are automatically rotated, unique per device, and centrally backed up.


Without LAPS enabled, endpoints and servers may rely on shared or static local administrator passwords. Attackers who obtain one such password can reuse it across multiple devices, enabling lateral movement, privilege escalation, and persistent administrative access.

Ensure that supported Windows devices have a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0 enabled and activated so Windows can use hardware-backed root-of-trust protections.


Without a working TPM 2.0, supported Windows devices lose a key hardware trust anchor for boot integrity, key protection, BitLocker readiness, Windows Hello scenarios, and other security features that rely on TPM-backed assurance.

Telnet as a management interface allows admins to remotely manage devices. Without an authentication requirement, any user who has network access to these devices may compromise them. Update the device configuration to require authentication.


Adversaries may be able to take full control of devices over the network if unauthenticated Test User 1 access is allowed.

Devices using SNMP V1 or V2 are vulnerable because SNMP V1 and V2 are not encrypted or secure communication protocols. Use a secure protocol such as SNMP V3 to administer devices.


Devices using SNMP V1 or V2 are at increased risk of credential theft.

VNC as a management interface allows admins to remotely manage devices. Without an authentication requirement, any user who has network access to these devices may compromise them. Update the device configuration to require authentication.


An attacker may be able to take full control of devices over the network if unauthenticated Test User 1 access is allowed.

Devices using Telnet are exposed to malicious threats because Telnet is not a secure and encrypted communication protocol. Use secure protocols such as SSH to administer devices.


Allowing devices to use Telnet increases their exposure to credential theft

Ensures that discovered devices in your network are protected by an endpoint security solution. Onboarding devices increases visibility and control of networks.


Devices inside the network that are not yet onboarded might be non-compliant with security levels recommended by your organization. These devices might introduce risk or open the network for attacks if they become compromised.
